name: Dutch East India Company

summary.text: The Verenigde Oostindische Compagnie (VOC) was a chartered trading company established in the Dutch Republic in 1602 by the States General, merging six smaller firms, with a monopoly over Dutch shipping and trade between the Cape of Good Hope and the Strait of Magellan and powers to make treaties, build forts and keep armed forces; its charter was ended and its debts absorbed by the state in 1799. The site links the VOC's merchants to the tulip mania of 1636–37; the sources consulted describe the VOC and the tulip episode separately and do not state a VOC role in the bulb trade or its 1637–38 settlement.

sources.title: Introduction to the Archives of the Verenigde Oostindische Compagnie

facts.claim: The VOC was set up in the Dutch Republic in 1602; its charter from the States General barred anyone except the VOC from sending ships from the Netherlands to, or trading in, the area east of the Cape of Good Hope and west of the Straits of Magellan.
facts.quote: The charter laid down that nobody except the VOC could send ships from The Netherlands to or conduct trade in the area east of the Cape of Good Hope and west of the Straits of Magellan.

sources.title: Introduction to the Archives of the Verenigde Oostindische Compagnie

facts.claim: In 1600 the Amsterdam companies trading to Asia amalgamated into one Geünieerde Amsterdamse Oostindische Compagnie, before the 1602 national charter.
facts.quote: In 1600 the Amsterdam companies amalgamated into one Geünieerde Amsterdamse Oostindische Compagnie.

sources.title: Introduction to the Archives of the Verenigde Oostindische Compagnie

facts.claim: Britannica dates the company from 1602 to 1799, when the state ended its charter and absorbed its debts and holdings.
facts.quote: Britannica's dates for the company are 1602 to 1799.

facts.claim: Britannica describes the tulip mania as largely contract-based, with sales and resales made many times over without bulbs leaving the ground, homes and businesses mortgaged to buy bulbs, and a collapse in early 1637.
facts.quote: Largely based on contracts, these sales and resales were often made many times over without the bulbs ever leaving the ground.

facts.claim: Garber (1989) records that florist delegates meeting in Amsterdam on 24 February 1637 proposed that contracts made on or before 30 November 1636 be executed while later buyers could withdraw for 10 percent of the price; the authorities did not adopt this, and on 27 April 1637 the States of Holland suspended all contracts, leaving buyers liable for the difference between resale price and whatever settlement price the authorities set.
facts.quote: The buyer would be responsible for the difference between this market price and whatever price the authorities eventually determined for contract settlement.

sources.publisher: Journal of Political Economy (Peter M. Garber, 1989; hosted copy)
sources.title: Tulipmania

facts.claim: Secondary accounts of Anne Goldgar's archival work state that Haarlem's council ruled in May 1638 that a buyer could walk away from a contract by paying 3.5 percent of the price, and that Goldgar found fewer than half a dozen people in financial trouble in the period, almost none attributable to tulips.
facts.quote: Haarlem's city council finally ruled in May 1638 that a buyer could walk away from a contract by paying 3.5 percent

sources.publisher: Encyclopaedia Romana (James Grout, University of Chicago hosted)
sources.title: Tulip Mania
Explaining the timing of tulipmania's boom and bust: historical context, sequestered capital and market signals

openQuestions: The site's '3.5% default fee' is supported as a Haarlem council resolution of May 1638 (per secondary accounts of Goldgar), not a conversion engineered by magistrates at the price peak; Garber's peer-reviewed account describes a 10% proposal by florists in February 1637 and a States of Holland suspension in April 1637. The claim that 'insider buyers' benefited is not stated by the sources.

No source consulted connects the VOC or 'VOC merchants' to the tulip trade or to the settlement; the site's insiders list ('Planter Elite', 'Amsterdam Notaries', 'Dutch Regents', 'VOC Merchants') is unsupported.
The 1636 plague as the crisis window was not addressed by the sources consulted.
Goldgar's own book (Tulipmania, 2007) should be checked directly for the Haarlem commission and 3.5 percent terms; only hosted summaries were returned.
